about.p: This book teaches more than 2,000 words and phrases at upper A2 and B1 level, chosen with the English Profile for their usefulness in everyday situations. Each unit has about 25 new items. The **left-hand page** presents them in short texts, tables, pictures and example sentences, with each new word explained straight after it appears. The **right-hand page** practises them, from easier exercises to harder ones, and ends with *Over to you*, where you write about yourself, your life and your country.
Units 1–4 are about learning vocabulary: keeping a notebook, using a dictionary and the words used to talk about language. Do them first. After that you can study the units in any order.

about.-: **Today** gives you new words every day from the next unit and brings them back for review. **Units** has each left-hand page and its practice; pass with 80%.
Write your *Over to you* answers in the app: they are saved and you can ask Claude to check them when it is available.

about.tip: The book recommends a vocabulary notebook organised by topic. On each word card you can write your own sentence; they are all collected in *My writing*.

L.p: Plan a study *routine* and keep to it: for example, one new unit every Sunday for *at least* half an hour, and a short session each morning to *revise* (go over again) what you learnt.
Be active: say each new word *aloud* and repeat it *silently*, highlight important words, write them in your notebook with an example from your own life.
Test yourself: cover the meaning and try to remember it. If you can't, check, then test yourself again five minutes later.
When you learn a word, look for *synonyms* (words with a similar meaning) and *opposites*, and notice its *word partners*: *take a break, take notes*.

L.h: A What dictionaries do I need?

L.p: A *bilingual* dictionary (one that uses two languages) gives you a fast answer. An English-only dictionary makes you read more English and shows the word in use. Many learners keep one of each.
A good dictionary shows the pronunciation in phonemic symbols, the part of speech, a definition, examples, common word partners and fixed phrases such as *for fun* and *make fun of somebody*.
Dictionaries use some words again and again to explain meanings.

L.p: *I* is a pronoun; *chair* and *window* are nouns; *have* is a verb; *brown* and *leather* are adjectives; *by* is a preposition; *the* is the definite article; *a* is the indefinite article.

When you learn a noun, check if it is *countable* (a chair, two chairs) or *uncountable* (*advice*, not *advices*). When you learn a verb, check if it is *irregular* (*buy – bought*). In *unhelpful*, *un-* is a *prefix* and *-ful* is a *suffix*.
*Book* has one syllable, *before* two, *cinema* three. In *before* the stress is on the second syllable. Every sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop or question mark.

L.p: The suffixes *-ion* and *-ment* form nouns from verbs: invent → invention, discuss → discussion, translate → translation, relax → relaxation, improve → improvement, govern → government, manage → management, develop → development.

L.p: Adjectives ending *-al* usually mean 'relating to the noun': a *musical* instrument, a *political* issue, an *electrical* fault, a *personal* opinion.

L.p: We form compound nouns by putting two (or three) words together: *ice hockey*, *public transport*, *campsite*, *babysitter*, *income tax*, *mother tongue*, *travel agent*, *film-maker*, *haircut*.

L.h: B Phrasal verbs with an object

L.e: You can say *Turn on the lamp* or *Turn the lamp on*. With *it*, *them*, etc. the pronoun goes in the middle: *Turn it on*.

units.sub: point of view, on the other hand, tend to

L.h: A The basis of a discursive essay

L.p: In a *discursive essay* you express your own *point of view*, show that you understand *both sides of an argument*, and use link words such as *in addition* and *however* (see Unit 93).

L.h: B Expressing a point of view

L.e: Some people believe that school uniforms should be abolished. There is an argument that public transport should be free for everyone.

L.tip: In written essays it is often better to use less personal phrases (*Some people believe…*, *There is an argument that…*) than *In my opinion*.

L.h: C Giving both sides of an argument

L.e: One of the advantages of working from home is that you save time. On the one hand, you have more freedom; on the other hand, you may feel isolated.
Compared with ten years ago, more people shop online. In contrast, the number of small shops has fallen.
On the whole, people tend to live longer than they did a century ago.
Too much screen time can affect sleep. Young people go to bed later and, consequently, find it hard to concentrate at school.

L.tip: The new rules will *affect* (not *effect*) all drivers. They will have a big *effect* (not *affect*) on traffic.

L.e: Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to ask about the evening Spanish classes on your website. I would be grateful if you could tell me the dates and the cost. I look forward to hearing from you. Yours faithfully, Sam Harris

L.e: Hi Tom, Just a quick message to say thanks for the birthday present – I love it! The party was a real laugh. I'm hoping to visit you in July, so I'll be in touch. Give my regards to your parents. All the best, Ana

L.tip: Start with *Hi*, *Hello* or *Dear*; end with *Love* or *Lots of love* (close friends and family) or *Best wishes* / *All the best* (friends).

L.e: It's been ages since we spoke! Just to let you know, we're having a barbecue on Saturday – would you like to join us? Anyway, I'd better go – the baby's crying.

L.tip: *Actually* means 'in fact', often adding a surprise: I thought she was French, but actually she's Belgian. For 'at this time', say: She's *currently* (not *actually*) living in Rome.

L.p: Most abbreviations are spoken as letters: *EU*, *UN*, *PM*, *MP*, *BBC*, *ID*, *PC*, *CV*. A few are spoken as words: *AIDS* /eɪdz/, *PIN* /pɪn/.

L.e: What does DIY stand for? – Do it yourself.

L.p: Some abbreviations are only written, and we say the full word: *Mr* (mister), *Mrs* (missus), *Dr* (doctor), *St* (Saint or Street).

L.h: C Abbreviations as part of the language

L.p: *etc.* = and so on; *e.g.* = for example; *i.e.* = that is to say, in other words.
Many words are shortened, especially in speech: phone, fridge, maths, exam, plane, photo, advert, flu, gym, lab, bike, TV or telly, vet, paper.
